name: Sui Dynasty
summary: A short dynasty that reunited China in 589 after nearly four centuries of division and built the Grand Canal.

location.value: Reunified all of China proper. The capitals were Daxing (Chang’an, modern Xi’an) from 581 to 605, and Luoyang from 605 to 618.

terrain.value: The Guanzhong heartland in the northwest, far from the rich eastern and southern economic centres, which the Grand Canal then linked together. Yellow River and Yangtze basins.

climate.value: Monsoonal. No specific climate shifts are recorded in the sources checked.

resources.value: A vast agricultural surplus, stored in large state granaries.

disasters.value: Floods along the Yellow River in the 610s worsened famine during the Goguryeo wars.

population.value: 46,019,956 people were registered in the census of 606 CE.

urbanisation.value: Two great planned capitals: the newly built Daxing (Chang’an) and the refounded Luoyang.

disease.value: No major epidemics are documented in the sources checked.

migration.value: Millions of workers were moved by forced labour drafts for canals and walls. Men are said to have broken their own limbs to avoid conscription.

economicBase.value: Agriculture under the equal-field land system, producing large surpluses.

tradeRoutes.value: The Grand Canal (605–609) linked Luoyang and Chang’an with Jiangdu (Yangzhou), Yuhang (Hangzhou) and the north near Beijing, the main north–south trade route for centuries.
tradeRoutes.source: Wikipedia: Sui dynasty (checked 5 Nov 2026); video research: RESEARCH.md, “5,000 Years of China”

wealth.value: No GDP estimate is available. State granaries were famously full under Emperor Wen.

moneyAndTax.value: Standardised and reunified the coinage (cash coins). Heavy taxation and compulsory labour duties under Emperor Yang.

inequality.value: A northwest military aristocracy dominated, while peasants carried the burden of labour drafts.

governmentType.value: An imperial monarchy. Emperor Wen abandoned the corrupt “nine-rank” recommendation system.

keyRulers.value: Emperor Wen (Yang Jian, 581–604). Emperor Yang (604–617/618). Emperor Gong (617–618).

succession.value: Yang Jian usurped the Northern Zhou throne in 581 and eliminated 59 Zhou princes. Emperor Yang’s succession in 604 may have involved murder.

institutions.value: The equal-field system. The Five Departments and Six Boards, forerunner of the Tang Three Departments and Six Ministries. Examinations for officials, which became the imperial examination system.

stability.value: Widespread revolts from 611 against taxes, labour drafts and the failed Korean wars.

eliteConflict.value: Emperor Yang was assassinated in 618 by a minister, Yuwen Huaji, and rival claimants were set up in different cities.

armyAndTech.value: Some 518,000 troops were reportedly massed on the Yangtze in 588. Large warships had five decks and could carry 800 non-crew personnel. The armies sent against Goguryeo were reportedly over one million strong (figures from a single account).

majorWars.value: The conquest of the Chen dynasty (589), reunifying China. The Linyi-Champa campaign (602–605). Failed campaigns against Goguryeo in Korea, which had ended in defeat by 614.

territoryChange.value: About 3 million km² in 589 (Wikipedia infobox), after the conquest of the south.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals were Goguryeo, the Turkic Khaganate (which Wen’s diplomacy split into eastern and western halves), Champa and the Tuyuhun.

inventions.value: Engineering on a massive scale: the Grand Canal, extensions of the Great Wall, and the rebuilding of Luoyang as a planned city.

scienceEducation.value: Revived examinations and state schools. Classical scholarship continued.

openness.value: Open to Buddhism and to Central Asian trade and culture (e.g. tombs of Sogdian merchants such as Yu Hong, 592).

religion.value: Buddhism was strongly promoted (Emperor Wen distributed relics in 601; the Tiantai school was founded by Zhiyi). Taoism, Confucianism, folk religion and Zoroastrianism were also present.

languageWriting.value: Middle Chinese. Emperor Wen created a special character (隋) for the dynasty’s name.

artsArchitecture.value: The planned capitals of Daxing and Luoyang, Buddhist cave sculpture, and early landscape painting (Zhan Ziqian, “Strolling About in Spring”).

socialStructure.value: Emperor, aristocratic clans of the northwest, officials, farming households owing taxes and labour, and dependants.

sharedIdentity.value: Restored a single Chinese state after nearly four centuries of division (220–589), a period in which Buddhism had spread widely.
sharedIdentity.source: Wikipedia: Sui dynasty (checked 5 Nov 2026); video research: RESEARCH.md, “5,000 Years of China”

neighbours.value: Goguryeo, the Turkic Khaganates, the Tuyuhun, Champa and northern Vietnam.

ideasReligions.value: Buddhism spread further with state support. Japanese embassies visited Sui China.

riseSignals.value: Reunited China in 589 after nearly four centuries of division (220–589). Northern Zhou had already reunified the north in 577. Wen’s reforms, granaries and standardised coinage.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Sui dynasty (checked 5 Nov 2026); video research: RESEARCH.md, “5,000 Years of China”

peakPeriod.value: Mid-dynasty prosperity around 600–610, with full granaries, the Grand Canal and the 606 census.

declineSignals.value: Costly canal works and forced labour, failed and very expensive invasions of Goguryeo (612–614), heavy taxes, floods and famine, then mass revolts.
declineSignals.source: Wikipedia: Sui dynasty (checked 5 Nov 2026); video research: RESEARCH.md, “5,000 Years of China”

outcome.value: Collapse. Emperor Yang was assassinated in 618, and Li Yuan founded the Tang dynasty (618), which kept most Sui institutions.

sources.value: The Book of Sui (Suishu), Tang-era histories (often hostile to Emperor Yang), and archaeology. Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026. See also Wright (1978).

overallCertainty.value: Good for the main events and the 606 census. Army sizes for the Korean wars are from single accounts and probably exaggerated. The end date is given as 618 or 619 depending on whether rival claimants are counted.
